author.name: Euripides
author.biography: Euripides made inherited myths speak through people under unbearable pressure. Ancient reports about his private life are often unreliable, but his surviving plays repeatedly give force to perspectives that a confident public account might prefer to silence. Euripides brought disturbing questions about marriage, foreigners and power before Athenian audiences. Medea gives a woman excluded from civic authority a voice that the men around her cannot safely ignore.

hook.text: What can being wronged make you feel entitled to do?

paragraphs: Jason has found a marriage that offers him a better future. Medea, who helped him reach his present position, is expected to accept the arrangement. She is a foreigner with children and very little protection.

Her account of what has been done to her is compelling. Euripides makes us hear the vulnerability built into marriage and dependence, and the ease with which a man can present his advantage as everybody's best interest. Sympathy comes quickly. It will not remain a simple guide.

The play presses on what happens when an injury becomes a claim to unlimited retaliation. Recognition matters: Medea wants Jason to understand the cost of treating her as someone who can be put aside. Other people stand between that desire and its fulfilment.
Read for the difficult distance between hearing a grievance and endorsing what follows from it. If the person who hurt you finally felt your pain, what would that repair?

orientation.text: The play begins after Jason has arranged a new marriage in Corinth. Medea's earlier help to him is part of the history both characters invoke.
